title: The Morning a Newspaper Decided I Wasn’t Big Enough
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis, a former senior finance executive now building her own company, describes the morning a newspaper pulled a planned feature because she lacked enough existing press and followers. Standing at an airport gate she gave herself a pep talk, which unsettled her because she had long believed motivation was just a story people tell themselves. She realizes the title she chased for twenty years was itself a story covering an older fear of being nobody, and that the corporate ladder had supplied her reasons for her. With no ladder, no quarterly number and no one defining success, she has to choose her own story out loud. Her test for telling stories apart is direction: harmful ones point backward at a fear, good ones point forward at something that does not yet exist, and she would rather be pulled by a story that might be true.
points: A leader who reads other people's hidden fears well can still be blind to the story driving her own ambition.
Titles and ladders supply motivation externally, so leaving them means authoring your own reasons.
Stories that point backward at a fear (a boss's gold star, her own title) distort behavior, while stories that point forward at a purpose sustain it.
Needing a story is not weakness; it is the cost of defining success for yourself.
quotes: The idea was good enough. I was not big enough. I needed press to earn press, I had none, and there was no way to turn nothing into something.
I thought motivation was a story people told themselves to explain why they were standing still. I believed that completely, I built a career on it, and I was proud of it.
For two decades the story was the title. Reach it and I would finally be someone. Hold it and no one could ask whether I belonged.
I could do that for anyone. Name the fear a person was hiding, and watch all of their behavior suddenly make sense. For everyone but the one person I could never read.
Corporate is a ladder, and the ladder does the work for you. There is always a next rung to reach for.
Needing the story is not weakness. It is what it costs when no one is defining success but me.
The harmful kind points backward, at a fear we are running from. The man’s gold star pointed at a doubt he could not face, and it made him cruel to everyone near him.
I would rather be pulled forward by a story that might be true than kept safe by one I already know is a lie.
